Get started

Source: vignettes/articles/ogis.qmd

ogis draws maps on MapLibre from data that stay in DuckDB: a parquet file, a lazy table, a data frame or an sf object. A map is built with the pipe, a layer at a time, and every map below is live: pan it, zoom it, click a point.

A first map

The example data are the positions of four vessels on the Icelandic groundfish survey in March 2019, one row a position, with whether a tow was on.

library(ogis)
positions <- og_example("trawlsurvey")
positions |> og_point(colour = behaviour)

colour takes a column written bare. Its values get a colour each and a legend; the map opens on the rows’ extent.

Layers with the pipe

og_map() starts a map from data, and each layer function adds a layer over the ones before. Here a line per vessel in the order of time, and the positions over it: two columns to colour by (the first shown; the other is a choice in the page), and a click that shows the row.

og_map(positions) |>
  og_path(group = vid, time = time, name = "Tracks") |>
  og_point(
    colour = c(behaviour, speed),
    popup = c(vid, time, speed, behaviour),
    name = "Positions"
  )

og_map() with no data starts a map whose layers bring their own. The survey’s tows are lines, one a row:

og_map() |>
  og_line(og_example("trawlsurveytows"), name = "Tows") |>
  og_point(positions, colour = behaviour, name = "Positions",
           visible = FALSE)

visible = FALSE leaves a layer off when the page opens; its box in the sidebar turns it on.

Rings and outlines

stroke draws each point as a ring of its colour, stroke pixels wide, hollow, size across; fill = NA an area’s outline alone. A click inside either still shows its row. Here the positions faster than 12 knots ringed over the others:

fast <- dplyr::filter(positions, speed > 12)
og_map(positions) |>
  og_point(colour = behaviour, name = "Positions") |>
  og_point(fast, colour = "#00a5c8", size = 14, stroke = 2,
           name = "Over 12 knots")

In MapLibre’s own terms

Every layer function takes MapLibre’s paint and layout properties by their own names, in quotes, for what its own arguments do not reach; and id, the name a page’s address and a script know the layer by. Here the tows dashed:

og_map() |>
  og_line(og_example("trawlsurveytows"), colour = "#4a5560", name = "Tows",
          "line-dasharray" = list(2, 1))

The order of layers

Each layer is drawn over the ones before it, whatever box of the sidebar it sits in (section). order in og_map() draws the layers it names first, by their id, under the others; the sidebar keeps its own order. Here the tows, listed last under Reference, drawn under the positions:

og_map(positions, order = "tows") |>
  og_point(colour = behaviour, name = "Positions") |>
  og_line(og_example("trawlsurveytows"), colour = "#4a5560", id = "tows",
          name = "Tows", section = "Reference")

Finding a row

search names a column whose values the page’s Find box, above the sidebar’s boxes, looks through: whole matches first, then values that begin with what is typed, then any that hold it, case and accents aside, each kind nearest the view’s centre first. A click on one takes the map there and shows its row. Here the tows by their id; type 4906:

og_map() |>
  og_line(og_example("trawlsurveytows"), popup = id.lgs, search = id.lgs,
          name = "Tows")

The sea floor

og_relief() draws a depth model’s depth in colour and its relief shaded; og_contour() the lines of equal depth, the charts’ depths a little heavier and labelled, thinner lines between. Here the Danish waters’ depths, made into tiles once by og_tiles_dem() and given to both, under the harbours:

depth <- og_tiles_dem(og_example("dansk_relief"), maxzoom = 6)
og_map(view = list(bounds = c(2.5, 54.5, 13, 58.5))) |>
  og_relief(depth) |>
  og_contour(depth) |>
  og_polygon(og_example("dansk_harbours"), fill = NA, colour = "#b2182b",
             name = "Harbours")

The arguments are where the map starts; the page’s controls, folded under ▸ beside each layer’s name, change the colours, the shading and the lines. The depth is grey at 75 % by default, quiet under the map’s own data; a map whose subject is the sea floor might start otherwise:

og_relief(depth, palette = "seabed", opacity = 100, limits = c(5, 60), shade = 0.8)
og_contour(depth, major = c(10, 20, 30, 50), minor = FALSE)

A depth model kept as an MBTiles file in its own place on each computer can be named once there, by a line in .Renviron (usethis::edit_r_environ() opens it), so a script shared between colleagues carries no path:

OGIS_DEPTH=D:/data/depth.mbtiles
og_map() |> og_relief() |> og_contour() # the model OGIS_DEPTH names

Values by cell

og_cells() colours a table of cells by a value per square kilometre, such as hours of fishing by cell, gear and year; the page has a control for each of the table’s other columns, and the colours’ own. As the page asks for a tile, DuckDB sums the cells under it to about a screen pixel at that zoom, the reader’s choices applied. Here the survey’s positions counted by 0.02-degree cell (each corner in thousandths of a degree), vessel and what it was doing; choose a vessel, or hauling:

by_cell <- positions |>
  dplyr::mutate(ix = floor(lon * 50) * 20, iy = floor(lat * 50) * 20, one = 1) |>
  dplyr::count(vid, behaviour, ix, iy, wt = one, name = "positions")
og_map() |>
  og_cells(by_cell, name = "Positions by cell",
           labels = c(vid = "Vessel", behaviour = "Doing", positions = "Positions"))

labels names the columns where the file’s data dictionary does not, as it can a gear’s code (codes). A column of years is chosen as a span, from and to; one_of names a column whose values are ways of counting the same thing (two definitions of fishing), shown one at a time. The arguments are where the map starts:

og_cells(effort, filter = list(gid = 6, year = c(2015, 2020)), one_of = "preset",
         palette = "blues", opacity = 60, limits = c(0.5, 300), name = "Fishing effort")

Place names

og_names() writes a list of place names, each from its own zoom (min_zoom), the larger first where they meet (level); the page’s Find box looks through them, accents aside and ð as d, and a click on one shows what else the table holds. Its controls, folded under ▸, set the names’ colour and the zoom they appear at; where the names have areas, those are a layer of their own. Here a few of Iceland’s bays and banks, at rough places:

places <- data.frame(
  name = c("Faxaflói", "Breiðafjörður", "Ísafjarðardjúp", "Húnaflói", "Skagafjörður",
           "Eyjafjörður", "Skjálfandi", "Þistilfjörður", "Vopnafjörður", "Selvogsbanki"),
  lon = c(-22.6, -23.1, -22.8, -20.6, -19.6, -18.3, -17.5, -15.4, -14.6, -21.6),
  lat = c(64.4, 65.25, 66.12, 65.8, 65.95, 65.95, 66.12, 66.2, 65.8, 63.6),
  min_zoom = c(5, 5, 6, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 6), level = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2),
  kind = c("bay", "bay", "fjord", "bay", "fjord", "fjord", "bay", "fjord", "fjord",
           "bank")
)
og_map() |>
  og_cells(by_cell, name = "Positions by cell",
           labels = c(vid = "Vessel", behaviour = "Doing", positions = "Positions")) |>
  og_names(places)

Type thistil in Find. A list of names kept as a file in its own place on each computer is named once, as the depth model is; and the cells too:

OGIS_NAMES=D:/data/ornefni.parquet
OGIS_CELLS=D:/data/effort.parquet
og_map() |>
  og_relief() |> og_contour() |> og_cells(name = "Fishing effort") |> og_names()

A layer of your own

What the layer functions do not draw, an og_layer() does, in MapLibre’s own terms: a style of your own on elevations, contours or tiles of your own. og_add_layer() puts one into the pipe, in a box of the sidebar of its own. Here the Danish depths again, in colour by a layer written out in full, as og_relief() writes it:

own <- og_layer(
  "depth", "dem", label = "Depth",
  tiles = og_tiles_dem(og_example("dansk_relief"), maxzoom = 6),
  style = list(list(id = "depth-colour", type = "color-relief")),
  colour = list(palette = "seabed", opacity = 75)
)
og_map(view = list(bounds = c(2.5, 54.5, 13, 58.5))) |>
  og_add_layer(own, section = "Sea floor") |>
  og_polygon(og_example("dansk_harbours"), fill = NA, colour = "#b2182b",
             name = "Harbours")

The harbours, their outlines alone, reach from Greenland to the Black Sea, so view opens the map on the grid’s box. Elevations and contours go under the base map’s place names, whatever their order in the pipe; the box Depth has the colours’ controls.

A base map of your own

A base map is a MapLibre style, or a picture’s tiles by address: by zoom and place ({z}/{x}/{y}), or a WMS’s GetMap with each tile’s box ({bbox-epsg-3857}). The first given is the one the map opens on, the others choices under Base map. Here GEBCO’s shaded sea floor from its WMS, which reaches past Europe’s seas, then ogis’s own:

gebco <- list(
  id = "gebco", label = "Sea floor (GEBCO)",
  attribution = "Imagery reproduced from the GEBCO Grid, GEBCO Compilation Group",
  tiles = paste0(
    "https://wms.gebco.net/mapserv?SERVICE=WMS&VERSION=1.3.0&REQUEST=GetMap",
    "&LAYERS=GEBCO_LATEST&STYLES=&FORMAT=image/png&CRS=EPSG:3857",
    "&WIDTH=256&HEIGHT=256&BBOX={bbox-epsg-3857}"
  )
)
og_map(positions, basemaps = c(list(gebco), og_basemaps())) |>
  og_point(colour = behaviour, name = "Positions")

A picture alone has no place names, and the layers’ texts are drawn in the browser’s own font. labels, a style’s address, puts that style’s names over it with its fonts, as on og_basemaps()’s, which take Carto’s.

Showing and sharing

  • In R, printing a map serves it on this computer and opens it in RStudio’s Viewer or a browser.
  • In a document (Quarto, R Markdown, a pkgdown article like this one), a printed map is drawn live in the page.
  • As a folder, og_bundle(map, "my-map") writes the map with its data, to open with a double click on any computer, with no R and no server.
